name: Argentina
summary: Argentine consulates do not issue a repatriation permit: the funeral home in the country of death prepares apostilled documents (death certificate, non-contagious disease certificate, embalming and sealed-coffin certificate) that travel with the coffin, and files the entry request with Argentine authorities.
documents: Death certificate (Argentine consulates in Australia ask for two copies), with Hague apostille
Certificate from the local health authority that the deceased did not die of a contagious disease, apostilled
Funeral home certificate of embalming and placement in a sealed, waterproof approved container or air tray, notarised where required and apostilled
Entry request filed by the funeral home with Argentine authorities stating date, place of shipment and destination
Passport or DNI of the deceased (recommended)
Some consulates (e.g. London) also ask for a local removal ('out of country') certificate and Spanish translations
coffin: Argentine consulates require the body to be prepared under international transport rules and placed in a sealed, waterproof coffin (or approved container / air tray), certified by the funeral home. No official specification of zinc lining or of an official witness to the sealing was found; in practice a metal-lined sealed coffin is used.
embalming: Required: Argentine consulates ask for a funeral home certificate confirming embalming (embalming report).
consular: All documents need a Hague apostille from the country of death (consular legalisation only for non-Hague countries); some consulates also require a Spanish translation. Argentine consulates state they do not legalise these documents and do not grant permits to repatriate remains: documents go directly to the airline. Argentina is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Registering the death at the consulate is advisable for civil records.
arrival: The Argentine funeral home receives the coffin and handles customs and health clearance and the burial or cremation under provincial or municipal rules. The national border health service (Direccion de Sanidad de Fronteras) is the competent health authority at ports of entry; current non-COVID filing rules are not published online, so confirm with the receiving funeral home.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. The aircraft must land at an international airport with customs, immigration and health services. Because the consulate process relies on the airline receiving the documents, on a charter the operator and the ground handler take that role: give them the apostilled originals and make sure the funeral home's entry request names the private flight and arrival airport.
private_jet_note: Make sure the entry request filed by the Argentine funeral home names the private flight and arrival airport.
export: An Argentine funeral home obtains the civil registry death certificate (usually within 1 to 3 days), the embalming certificate and the certificate permitting transfer of the remains abroad, and supplies the special international casket. The destination country decides whether Argentine documents need an apostille. If a judge is involved (autopsy, violent or unexplained death) the judge must release the body and may delay it until test results are in; UK guidance says local formalities usually take 2 to 4 weeks.
export_points: Funeral home gathers death certificate, embalming and transfer certificates
Judicial release needed when a court is involved
Apostille as required by destination country
Typically 2 to 4 weeks according to UK guidance

at_a_glance.death_certificate: Apostilled; Spanish translation may be asked
at_a_glance.coffin: Sealed, waterproof coffin certified by funeral home
at_a_glance.consular: Apostille only; consulate issues no permit
at_a_glance.permit: Argentine funeral home files entry request
at_a_glance.arrival: Argentine funeral home clears customs and health

steps.what: Register the death locally and appoint a funeral home there and a receiving funeral home in Argentina
Obtain the death certificate and a health authority certificate of no contagious disease
Embalming and placement in a sealed waterproof coffin; funeral home certificate issued
Apostille all documents; Argentine funeral home files the entry request
Receiving funeral home clears customs and health and arranges burial or cremation

key_points: Argentine consulates do not issue a repatriation permit
Every foreign document needs a Hague apostille
Embalming certificate is required
Confirm current health filing rules with the receiving funeral home
authority: Direccion de Sanidad de Fronteras (Ministry of Health) at the border; Argentine funeral home files the entry request

name: Bolivia
summary: No official Bolivian page on bringing a body into Bolivia was found. Expect the usual Latin American path: apostilled death certificate, embalming and non-contagious disease certificates, a hermetically sealed coffin, and a Bolivian funeral home receiving the coffin; confirm with the Bolivian consulate covering the place of death.
documents: Death certificate, apostilled (Bolivia is a Hague Apostille party), with Spanish translation (to confirm)
Embalming certificate (to confirm)
Certificate of no contagious disease (to confirm)
Funeral home certificate on the sealed coffin and its contents (to confirm)
Passport or ID of the deceased
coffin: Not published for incoming remains. Bolivia itself requires a special hermetically sealed coffin (inner metal casket in an outer wooden container) for remains leaving the country, so plan the same standard for entry and confirm with the consulate.
embalming: Not published for incoming remains; expect embalming to be required. Bolivian rules for outgoing remains require embalming and formaldehyde preservation certified by the Ministry of Health or a prosecutor's or police doctor.
consular: No official Bolivian consular page on repatriation of remains could be opened. Ask the Bolivian consulate covering the place of death whether it registers the death, legalises or visas the documents, or issues a transfer authorisation. Bolivia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: At Bolivian airports, documents for remains are checked by the international health department, customs and the anti-narcotics unit (stated for outgoing remains; expect similar checks on arrival). A Bolivian funeral home should collect the coffin. Burial requires a Ministry of Health burial authorisation.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs, health and anti-narcotics control (for example La Paz El Alto, Santa Cruz Viru Viru) and arrange for the receiving funeral home to meet the aircraft.
private_jet_note: Expect customs and anti-narcotics checks on the coffin at arrival.
export: Procedures are very bureaucratic. A local funeral home (only some undertakers handle repatriations) gathers: forensic doctor's medical death certificate, civil registry death certificate, identification and autopsy reports if applicable, a formolisation (formaldehyde preservation) certificate from the Ministry of Health or prosecutor's/police doctor, a repatriation permission certificate from the Ministry of Health Epidemiology Department naming the airline and flight itinerary, a funeral home certificate that the hermetically sealed coffin (inner metal, outer wood) complies and contains no drugs, weapons or explosives, and the air waybill. Authorisations must be legalised by the Ministry of Health and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Documents are checked at the airport by health, customs and anti-narcotics. Local formalities normally take 8 to 10 days.
export_points: Ministry of Health Epidemiology permit with flight itinerary
Embalming plus formaldehyde certificate required
Hermetic metal-lined coffin; no drugs or weapons certificate
Usually 8 to 10 days; legalisation by Health and Foreign Affairs

steps.what: Contact the Bolivian consulate covering the place of death and appoint a receiving funeral home in Bolivia
Obtain the death certificate and medical certificates; apostille them
Embalming and sealing in a hermetic metal-lined coffin with outer wooden case
Complete any consular formalities and book the flight
Health, customs and anti-narcotics checks; funeral home collects and obtains burial authorisation

key_points: No official entry rules published online; confirm with consulate
Outgoing remains need a Ministry of Health permit
Allow 8 to 10 days to send a body out of Bolivia
authority: Ministry of Health (Epidemiology Department); Bolivian consulates abroad

name: Brazil
summary: Under ANVISA resolution RDC 662/2022, human remains must have been preserved (embalming or formalinisation), with a signed conservation record, travel in a sealed zinc-lined (or equivalent) impermeable wooden urn without a window, and be carried in the cargo compartment. Brazilian consulates register the death and handle the transfer documents; foreign documents are apostilled.
documents: Local death certificate, apostilled (Brazilian consulates also issue a consular death registration)
Conservation record (Ata de Conservacao de Restos Mortais Humanos) or equivalent embalming certificate, attached by the carrier to the transport documents (RDC 662/2022 Art. 6)
Certificate that the death was not caused by a contagious disease (usually asked by consulates; to confirm)
Transit or removal permit from the country of death
Passport of the deceased and air waybill
coffin: RDC 662/2022 defines the funeral urn as an outer wooden box lined inside with zinc sheets or an equivalent material, impermeable and without a viewing window. The ANVISA conservation record model states the remains are placed in the impermeable urn which is then sealed in front of the signatories (family representative, doctor, assistant and two witnesses).
embalming: Mandatory: remains must have undergone a conservation procedure (formalinisation, embalming or another method set by ANVISA or the Ministry of Health), recorded in a conservation record (RDC 662/2022 Art. 5 and 6). Conservation and transfer are prohibited when death was caused by spongiform encephalopathy, haemorrhagic fever or another new infectious disease designated by WHO and the Ministry of Health (Art. 8).
consular: Foreign documents are normally apostilled. Brazilian consulates register the death and usually handle documents for the transfer; the exact list varies by consulate (official consulate pages could not be opened for this check). Brazil is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Families pay; since 2025 the Foreign Ministry may fund repatriation only in exceptional cases.
arrival: ANVISA carries out sanitary control of remains at airports only in public health emergencies or risk situations (Art. 3), but the documents must be available whenever requested (Art. 4). A Brazilian funeral company receives the urn, clears customs and arranges burial or cremation under municipal rules. Ashes are not subject to sanitary control.
private_aviation: RDC 662/2022 Art. 5 requires human remains to travel in the cargo compartment of the means of transport. Many business jets have no hold able to take a zinc-lined coffin, so check with the operator and ANVISA (port, airport and border health service at the arrival airport) before planning a cabin-loaded casket. Keep the conservation record and all documents on board.
private_jet_note: Brazil requires remains to travel in the cargo compartment; confirm aircraft suitability first.
export: A Brazilian funeral company arranges conservation (embalming or formalinisation) with the ANVISA conservation record, the zinc-lined urn, the notary-issued death certificate and a Federal Police authorisation document, and meets the destination country's consular requirements. Autopsy results can take a few weeks and cremation needs a judge's approval.
export_points: Conservation record and zinc-lined urn required
Federal Police authorisation document
Death certificate from local notary (cartorio)
Remains must travel in the cargo compartment

at_a_glance.coffin: Sealed zinc-lined wooden urn, no window
at_a_glance.permit: Documents shown to ANVISA on request
at_a_glance.arrival: Cargo compartment only; funeral company collects

steps.what: Contact the Brazilian consulate and appoint funeral homes at both ends
Obtain the local death certificate and permits; apostille them
Embalming or formalinisation; conservation record signed; urn sealed in front of witnesses
Consular death registration and transfer documents; book cargo-hold transport
Documents available to ANVISA; Brazilian funeral company collects the urn

key_points: Conservation record is compulsory
Zinc-lined urn without a window
Cargo compartment rule matters for private jets
Ashes are not subject to sanitary control
authority: ANVISA (port, airport and border health control); Brazilian consulates abroad

name: Chile
summary: Under Chile's General Cemeteries Regulation (Decree 357 of 1970), a body may enter Chile only with documents from the health authority of the place of origin, endorsed by the Chilean consul, showing the transport poses no public health risk, and with authorisation of the competent Regional Ministerial Health Secretary (SEREMI de Salud).
documents: Death certificate, apostilled or legalised, with Spanish translation (to confirm with the consulate)
Health authority document from the place of origin stating the transport poses no public health risk, endorsed (visado) by the Chilean consul (Decree 357 Art. 78)
Embalming certificate (to confirm)
Authorisation of the competent SEREMI de Salud for international transport and entry (Art. 75)
Passport of the deceased
coffin: Coffins used to transport bodies must be impermeable and able to be hermetically closed (Art. 67); burial in a vault or niche requires a hermetically sealed coffin (Art. 51). A metal-lined sealed coffin with an outer wooden case is the practical standard.
embalming: Not expressly required for entry in the regulation; in practice expected for international transport. Bodies normally must be buried within 48 hours unless embalmed with health authority approval or a judicial or health order applies (Art. 48), so embalming matters for the timing in Chile.
consular: Decree 357 requires the origin health documents to be endorsed by the Chilean consul. Chile has joined the Hague Apostille Convention, so ask the consulate whether an apostille now replaces the consular endorsement. Chile is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: The SEREMI de Salud authorises the entry and transfer. Funeral homes may not change coffins or move bodies without health authority authorisation (Art. 66). A Chilean funeral home collects the coffin; burial needs the civil registry burial pass. Cremation needs SEREMI authorisation and, after an accident or suspected crime, judicial authorisation.
private_aviation: Decree 357 Art. 77 requires a coffin moved between cities or abroad to travel in a separate compartment of the aircraft under the captain's responsibility. A coffin in the passenger cabin of a business jet may not satisfy this; check with the SEREMI de Salud and the operator. Land at an international airport with customs, police and health services.
private_jet_note: Chilean rules require the coffin in a separate aircraft compartment under the captain's responsibility.
export: The SEREMI de Salud authorises international transport (Decree 357 Art. 75). The health authority checks that the coffin is impermeable and in good condition, draws up a record, seals the coffin and issues the authorisation; the seal may not be removed before arrival at destination (Art. 77). The civil registry death certificate is usually issued within 24 to 72 hours. If a judge is involved the body is released only when the judge is satisfied; straightforward cases take one to two weeks according to UK guidance.
export_points: SEREMI de Salud authorisation and seal on the coffin
Coffin travels in a separate compartment of the aircraft
Judicial release needed after violent or unexplained death
Usually one to two weeks

at_a_glance.laissez_passer: Origin health document endorsed by Chilean consul
at_a_glance.arrival: Funeral home collects; SEREMI authorises transfer

name: Colombia
summary: Colombia's 111 consulates guide families on repatriating a body or ashes, but no official Colombian list of entry documents could be opened. Expect an apostilled death certificate, embalming and non-contagious disease certificates and a hermetically sealed coffin; confirm with the Colombian consulate covering the place of death.
documents: Death certificate, apostilled, with Spanish translation (to confirm)
Embalming certificate (to confirm)
Certificate of no contagious disease (to confirm)
Transit or removal permit from the country of death
Funeral home certificate on the sealed coffin contents (to confirm)
Passport of the deceased
coffin: No official Colombian specification found; a hermetically sealed metal-lined coffin with outer wooden case is the usual standard for international air transport. Confirm with the consulate.
embalming: Not confirmed from an official source; expect embalming to be required. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: Colombian consulates advise families (Decree 869 of 2016 limits the Foreign Ministry's role to advice and assistance). The state has no budget for repatriation; the Foreign Ministry cites costs of USD 10,000 to 30,000 and recommends travel insurance. When a family cannot pay, ashes may in some cases be sent by diplomatic bag to the Ministry in Bogota. Colombia is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: A Colombian funeral home should receive the coffin, clear customs and health checks and arrange burial or cremation. The arrival health formalities are not published online; confirm with the receiving funeral home.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs, migration and health services (for example Bogota El Dorado) and arrange for the receiving funeral home to meet the aircraft with all original documents on board.
export: Formal identification by the Instituto Nacional de Medicina Legal must be completed before repatriation can start (weeks, or months if DNA is needed). The Fiscalia (prosecutor) must confirm the body can be released. The Registraduria death certificate is usually ready in about 2 days and should be apostilled by the Foreign Ministry. The local funeral director, acting under a power of attorney and written next-of-kin consent, arranges embalming and transfer to Bogota for the flight. Cremation requires prosecutor authorisation and is only possible for natural deaths or after a full autopsy.
export_points: Medicina Legal identification comes first
Prosecutor must release the body
Apostille the death certificate at the Foreign Ministry
Remains usually flown out from Bogota

steps.what: Contact the Colombian consulate and appoint funeral homes at both ends
Obtain death certificate and medical certificates; apostille and translate them
Embalming and sealing in a hermetic coffin
Confirm document list with the consulate and book the flight

key_points: Entry document list not published; confirm with consulate

authority: Colombian consulates (Ministry of Foreign Affairs); Ministry of Health and port health authorities

name: Ecuador
summary: No official Ecuadorian page on bringing a body into Ecuador was found. Expect an apostilled death certificate, embalming and non-contagious disease certificates and a hermetically sealed coffin, with the Ministry of Public Health as competent health authority; confirm with the Ecuadorian consulate covering the place of death.
documents: Death certificate, apostilled, with Spanish translation (to confirm)
Embalming certificate (to confirm)
Certificate of no contagious disease (to confirm)
Funeral home certificate that the coffin meets health rules (to confirm)
Passport of the deceased
Air waybill
coffin: Not published for incoming remains; a hermetically sealed metal-lined coffin with outer wooden case is the usual standard. Confirm with the consulate.
embalming: Not published for incoming remains; expect embalming to be required. For outgoing remains, Ecuadorian law requires some organs to be removed, treated and returned to the body before repatriation.
consular: No official Ecuadorian consular page could be opened. Ask the Ecuadorian consulate whether it registers the death, legalises documents or issues a transfer authorisation. Ecuador is a Hague Apostille party and not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement.
arrival: A local funeral home should receive the coffin and handle customs and Ministry of Public Health formalities. Arrival rules are not published online; confirm with the receiving funeral home.
private_aviation: No rule specific to private flights was found. Land at an international airport with customs and health services (Quito or Guayaquil) and arrange for the receiving funeral home to meet the aircraft. For outgoing remains, the Ministry of Public Health permit is issued to the airline with a flight itinerary, so on a charter make sure the operator and flight details are on the permit.
private_jet_note: For flights out of Ecuador, the health permit must show the private flight's itinerary.
export: Required: medical death certificate from a legal doctor on the INEC form, civil registry (Registro Civil) death certificate, certificate of organ removal and embalming, a repatriation permission certificate from the Ministry of Public Health Epidemiology Department issued to the airline and funeral director with the flight itinerary, the funeral director's certificate that the coffin meets health regulations, the passport and the air waybill. Next of kin may need to identify the deceased (in person or by video). Post-mortems are required for sudden, violent or unexplained deaths. Cremation is not allowed after violent deaths.
export_points: Ministry of Public Health repatriation permit with itinerary
Organs removed, treated and returned before embalming
Registro Civil death certificate
No cremation after violent deaths

at_a_glance.arrival: Funeral home clears customs and health

Obtain death certificate and medical certificates; apostille and translate them
Embalming and sealing in a hermetic coffin

name: Falkland Islands
summary: The Falkland Islands are a UK Overseas Territory with their own laws; no official Falklands rule on bringing a coffin in was found. Contact the Falkland Islands Government Registry Services and Customs and Immigration before arranging the flight.
documents: Death certificate, with English translation if needed (to confirm)
Embalming certificate (to confirm)
Certificate of no contagious disease (to confirm)
Funeral director's certificate of contents of the sealed coffin (to confirm)
Passport of the deceased
coffin: Not published; a hermetically sealed metal-lined coffin with outer wooden case is the usual standard for air transport.
embalming: Not published; expect embalming to be required for the long journey.
consular: Not applicable as such: the Falklands are a British Overseas Territory, so there is no Falklands consulate. The UK is not a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement. Confirm documents with Falkland Islands Government Registry Services.
arrival: The Registry office in Stanley registers deaths for the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands; sudden or unnatural deaths go to the Coroner. Rules for receiving a coffin from abroad, customs clearance and burial are not published online; contact Registry Services and Customs and Immigration.
private_aviation: Any aircraft landing in the Falklands needs a Foreign Carrier Permit from the Falkland Islands Civil Aviation Department (FICAD); charters use a Short Term permit (up to 14 days) and private flights a Letter of Permission carried on board. Apply at least 14 days before the flight (medical flights excepted). Prior permission is required to land at either international airport, Stanley (SFAL) or Mount Pleasant (EGYP). UK-registered aircraft need no permit but must still notify FICAD.
private_jet_note: Foreign Carrier Permit and landing permission needed; apply at least 14 days ahead.
export: Not published. The death must be registered at the Registry in Stanley (within 5 days in Stanley, 14 days elsewhere); deaths referred to the Coroner are registered only once the Coroner provides the information. Ask Registry Services and the Coroner about release of the body and documents for removal abroad.
export_points: Register the death at the Registry in Stanley
Coroner involvement for sudden or unnatural deaths
Removal rules not published; contact Registry Services

at_a_glance.death_certificate: Not published; confirm with Registry Services
at_a_glance.arrival: Not published; contact Registry and Customs

steps.what: Contact Falkland Islands Government Registry Services and Customs and Immigration
Apply to FICAD for the aircraft permit and landing permission (14 days ahead)
Obtain death certificate, embalming and coffin certificates at the place of death
Seal the coffin and confirm receipt arrangements in Stanley
Customs clearance and handover to the local undertaker

key_points: Aircraft permit must be requested at least 14 days ahead
Only Stanley and Mount Pleasant accept international flights
No published rules for incoming coffins
authority: Falkland Islands Government (Registry Services; Customs and Immigration; Civil Aviation Department)

name: French Guiana
summary: French Guiana is a French overseas department and follows French rules: entry of a body from abroad is authorised by the French embassy or consulate in the country of departure, and an airtight (metal-lined) coffin is mandatory for air transport.
documents: Local death certificate (transcription into French civil status recommended)
Medical certificate of cause of death or non-contagious disease (usually asked)
Embalming or conservation certificate where the departure country requires it
Body transport authorisation issued by the French embassy or consulate
Burial or cremation arrangements in French Guiana (receiving funeral director)
coffin: An airtight coffin (in practice a soldered zinc lining inside a wooden coffin) is mandatory for air transport under French rules. A hermetic coffin complicates cremation, so decide on cremation before departure.
embalming: France sets no single rule for incoming bodies; embalming is normally required by the departure country and airlines for long journeys. Confirm with the consulate.
consular: The French embassy or consulate in the country of death issues the authorisation to transport the body or ashes and can transcribe the foreign death certificate. Families pay all costs. France is a party to the 1973 Strasbourg Agreement; whether its laissez-passer is used for French Guiana was not confirmed, and none of the neighbouring South American countries is a party.
arrival: The receiving funeral director takes charge of the coffin at the airport. French law sets a 14-day maximum for burial or cremation (decree 2024-790, extendable to 21 days by the prefect); for deaths abroad it runs from entry of the body into France. How this is counted for arrival in an overseas department was not confirmed; ask the Prefecture of French Guiana.
private_aviation: The French airtight-coffin rule applies to any air transport, including private flights. Land at Cayenne Felix Eboue (the international airport with customs) and arrange for the receiving funeral director to meet the aircraft. The documents travel with the coffin.
private_jet_note: An airtight zinc-lined coffin is mandatory for any flight into French Guiana.
export: A funeral director handles the procedure. Transport of a body out of French Guiana, abroad or to mainland France, is authorised by the prefect of the department where the coffin is closed (Prefecture of French Guiana). An airtight coffin is mandatory by air. Ashes need authorisation from the prefect of the place of cremation or of the applicant's residence. The destination country's consular rules also apply.
export_points: Prefect of French Guiana authorises transport
Airtight coffin mandatory by air
Ashes: prefect authorisation
Check destination consulate requirements

at_a_glance.coffin: Airtight metal-lined coffin mandatory by air
